sets.name: Unit 01 Reading 1 손 씻기가 사람을 살린다고?!
sents: Not all medical breakthroughs are recognized at the time they are made.
Ignaz Semmelweis, a Hungarian physician, experienced this firsthand when his insights into the role of hygiene in preventing infection were dismissed by other healthcare professionals.
Until the mid-19th century, death during childbirth was alarmingly common throughout Europe.
No one understood why until 1847, when Semmelweis made an important observation at his hospital—pregnant women had higher mortality rates when treated by doctors than by midwives.

Convinced that doctors who had performed autopsies were transferring harmful substances to the women, Semmelweis ordered them to wash their hands with a chlorinated lime solution before assisting with childbirth.
The results were immediate and dramatic: mortality rates dropped from 18 percent to less than 2 percent.
Despite this remarkable outcome, Semmelweis faced strong resistance from his fellow physicians, who were offended by the idea that they themselves could be causing their patients harm.

Frustrated by the rejection of his ideas, Semmelweis publicly criticized members of the medical community in open letters that circulated across Europe, even accusing them of being careless murderers.
This led to struggles in his professional life, and he was eventually committed to an asylum, where he died in 1865.

Semmelweis’s findings were validated by later scientists like Louis Pasteur, credited with developing modern germ theory, and Joseph Lister, who invented an antiseptic system for use during surgeries.
Today, the principle of hygiene that Semmelweis pioneered has evolved into standard medical practices that significantly reduce infection rates in hospitals.

sets.name: Unit 01 Reading 2 예쁜데 별도 만들어?
sents: Imagine factories—not producing cars or smartphones, but twinkling stars.
Deep within the Eagle Nebula lies one such “factory” known as the Pillars of Creation.
Located about 6,500 light-years from Earth, the Pillars of Creation are three towering celestial formations—spanning nearly five light-years—that resemble rocky cliffs.
In reality, they are made of dense clouds of gas and dust.
They get their name from the role they play as a star nursery.
These cosmic regions are where new stars are born and nurtured over millions of years.
The Pillars of Creation were first observed in visible light by the Hubble Telescope in 1995.
Then, in 2022, more advanced infrared images taken by the James Webb Space Telescope revealed that the pillars themselves have been shaped in part by a set of nearby young stars.
As these stars are born and grow, they emit energy that clears away light dust and gas, leaving only the denser clouds that form the pillars.
The Pillars of Creation are so fascinating and beautiful that they have appeared in movies and television shows, on T-shirts and pillows, and even on a postage stamp.
Furthermore, they provide crucial data for astronomers, helping them to refine models of star formation and deepening our understanding of how stars form and evolve.

sets.name: Unit 01 Reading 3 기왕 넘은 거, 내가 책임질게
sents: For a long time, environmental ethics emphasized one clear principle: humans should leave nature alone.
Interfering with natural processes was seen as harmful, even when done with good intentions.
This idea became widely accepted, shaping how people thought about conservation, wildlife protection, and even scientific research.
Recently, however, this principle has begun to lose its certainty.
Many scientists and ethicists now argue that humans have already crossed too many boundaries to claim the role of distant observers.
Large-scale development, climate change, and genetic engineering have altered ecosystems so deeply that the idea of an untouched natural world is increasingly unrealistic.
From this perspective, human involvement is no longer an exception—it is the norm.
Even actions meant to protect nature, such as listing species as endangered or restoring damaged habitats, involve deliberate human decisions.
Doing nothing, in such cases, does not preserve nature as it once was; it simply allows existing damage to continue.
As a result, a growing number of voices suggest that the ethical question has shifted.
Instead of asking whether humans should intervene in nature at all, they ask how humans should intervene responsibly.
If humans have already reshaped the natural world, then careful, limited intervention may not be a violation of nature, but a duty arising from past actions.
In many cases, choosing not to act can still shape outcomes in the natural world.
Even so, this does not mean that the call to “leave nature alone” has disappeared.
Some still warn that intervention risks repeating the same mistakes that caused harm in the first place.
Yet the debate reflects a changing reality: the question is no longer whether to act, but how to act responsibly.

sets.name: Unit 01 Reading 4 The One Word That Defines a Nation
sents: Can you describe the people of your nation using only one word?
It seems like a difficult task, but the people of Finland can do it easily.
Ask any Finnish person, and the answer will always be the same, sisu!
But what exactly is sisu?
It derives from an old Finnish word for one’s physical courage in times of war but has developed over time into a larger concept that includes mental and emotional strength.
It is traditionally seen as having three main elements.
The first is extraordinary perseverance in the face of seemingly overwhelming odds.
The second is having the quality of being action-oriented, or being someone who will do whatever is necessary without worrying about the risk of failure.
Finally, sisu is closely linked to the idea of inner strength—it is like a hidden well of power that can be drawn upon in times of physical or mental duress.
While sisu had long been in the backdrop of Finnish society, it experienced a resurgence after Finland achieved independence from Russia in 1917.
By this time, weary from centuries of occupation by various foreign powers, the Finnish public needed something positive to rally around.
Finnish intellectuals seized upon the idea of sisu and helped revive it in the national consciousness.
This proved fortunate when the newly formed Soviet Union invaded Finland in 1939.
Badly outnumbered but filled with sisu, the Finns exacted heavy losses on the Soviet side, thus discovering that sisu functioned almost as a collective survival strategy.

sets.name: Unit 02 Reading 1 갑자기 신이 나타나서 다 해결해 준다고?
sents: At the end of The Lord of the Rings, two hobbits complete an exhausting journey and fulfill their mission, only to face certain death as lava closes in around them.
Then, without warning, giant eagles appear and carry them to safety.
If this resolution felt somewhat unsatisfying, you may have encountered what is known as deus ex machina.
The term, derived from Latin, means “a god from the machine”.
In ancient Greek theater, gods were sometimes lowered onto the stage by mechanical devices, resolving otherwise impossible situations and signaling that the play had reached its end.
At the time, this technique was not intended to feel realistic, but rather to bring the story to a clear conclusion.
In modern storytelling, however, deus ex machina is often viewed critically.
When a problem is solved by an unexpected force introduced without sufficient buildup, audiences may feel that the narrative has violated its own logic.
What causes dissatisfaction is not the presence of a miraculous resolution, but the sense in the audience that it has not been earned.
Yet, some writers employ deus ex machina deliberately.
Instead of aiming to satisfy the audience, they may choose to leave them unsettled, encouraging viewers to imagine a more convincing ending—one the author deliberately leaves open.
In this way, an abrupt resolution can redirect attention away from the solution itself and toward the questions that remain unanswered.
A story, then, does not always exist to comfort its audience.
In some cases, it seeks to ensure that the thinking continues long after the ending has arrived.

sets.name: Unit 02 Reading 2 플라스틱의 천적이 될 테야!
sents: Despite efforts to curb plastic consumption, global production still exceeds 380 million tons annually.
This has prompted scientists to explore unconventional solutions, including the use of plastic-eating bacteria.

In 2016, a team of Japanese scientists discovered Ideonella sakaiensis (I. sakaiensis), a bacterium with the ability to break down polyethylene terephthalate (PET), the plastic commonly used in bottles and packaging, within a laboratory setting.
This bacterium secretes a special enzyme that degrades plastic in order to metabolize the carbon within it as an energy source.
When placed in a dry container with a small piece of plastic weighing only 200 milligrams, the bacteria took about seven weeks to consume it.
However, such a long time was disappointing given the results obtained.
Fortunately, other scientists believe they have found a way to address this issue—genetically modifying bacteria to accelerate plastic decomposition.
One approach involves genetically modifying the enzyme produced by I. sakaiensis.
By applying thousands of random mutations to the enzyme and then evaluating their effects, researchers hope to create a version of the bacterium that can break down plastic quickly and effectively.
Genetic research may also enable I. sakaiensis to function in a marine environment, where large amounts of microplastics have accumulated.
Scientists are attempting to integrate the DNA of I. sakaiensis with that of Vibrio natriegens, a bacterium known to thrive in salt water.
If these experiments are successful, it could pave the way for removing plastic waste from the planet’s oceans in the future.

sets.name: Unit 02 Reading 3 불가능을 깨뜨린 4분의 기적
sents: When everyone said it was impossible, one runner stood on the athletic track with the conviction to achieve what no one had done before.
Born in England in 1929, Roger Bannister was a gifted young man.
While studying at Oxford University Medical School to become a doctor, he also devoted time to pursuing an entirely different passion—running.
His natural talent and consistent effort led him to win the British championship in the mile in 1951, which resulted in him qualifying for the Helsinki Olympics the following year.
Unfortunately, he failed to achieve the goal of winning a gold medal and finished in fourth place.
However, Bannister refused to let this setback dull his passion; he aimed for an even greater goal—breaking the “four-minute barrier” in the mile.
At that time, some experts claimed that running that fast could put excessive strain on the heart, potentially leading to death.
However, he believed that his steady approach to training—one hour of running, five days a week—would allow him to break the barrier.
After relentless efforts, on May 6, 1954, Bannister participated in a mile race.
Finally, for the first time in human history, he crossed the finish line in under 4 minutes, with a record of 3 minutes 59.4 seconds.
Although his record was broken less than two months later, his spirit of challenge has inspired others to achieve what was previously thought impossible in human performance.

sets.name: Unit 02 Reading 4 Why Bother Counting the Cold?
sents: Unlike today, the Roman New Year did not begin on January 1.
In ancient Rome, it began in March, when the ground thawed and activities such as farming and warfare could begin.
Winter—a season in which little to no activity took place—was left out entirely and simply passed without being recorded.
Over time, however, this unrecorded winter period began to cause problems.
Even then, a year was understood to be about 365 days long, and each month was estimated to last roughly 29 to 31 days.
In other words, although 12 months elapsed in a full year, the Roman calendar displayed only 10.
Because of this mismatch, the beginning and end of the year were not clearly defined, leading to confusion in administrative matters and in the dates of religious events.
To address this issue, King Numa Pompilius reformed the Roman calendar in around 713 BC.
He incorporated the previously excluded winter period by adding two new months.
But instead of being placed at the end, they were added to the beginning, reflecting the Roman belief that winter marked both the end of one year and a time of preparation for the next.
Among the newly added months, January was named after Janus, the god of doors and beginnings.
Janus had two faces, one looking back to the past and another toward the future, symbolizing a moment that is both an ending and a beginning.

In this way, winter came to be seen not as an empty stretch of time, but as a transitional period, and January ultimately took its place at the start of the calendar as the month that opens the new year.

sets.name: Unit 03 Reading 1 사자 옆집에 삽니다~
sents: In West Africa’s Sahel, human settlements emerged alongside savannas inhabited by large wild animals.
Unlike societies in which farmland and wildlife habitats were clearly separated, communities in this region shared daily living space with elephants, lions, and antelopes.
Consequently, early West African kingdoms could not regard wildlife as a distant or purely external force.
Wild animals were a constant presence, posing both danger and opportunity in everyday life.
Rather than attempting to eliminate wildlife or impose direct control over it, these kingdoms developed social mechanisms that regulated human interaction with animals.
Hunting was not viewed as an individual choice but as an activity shaped by communal expectations.
Certain animals were protected through long-standing traditions, while others could be hunted only during designated seasons.
Such practices were sustained not by written laws or formal administrative bodies, but by shared customs, religious beliefs, and collective social pressure.
The authority to oversee these arrangements typically rested with local leaders, chiefs, or kings.
Their power did not derive from direct ownership of land or animals.
Instead, it was exercised through the regulation of access—determining who was permitted to hunt, when hunting could occur, and which animals could be targeted.
Furthermore, by controlling access to valuable resources such as ivory or meat from large game, rulers reinforced their political legitimacy and preserved social order.
This relationship with wildlife shaped the broader organization of society.
Because survival depended on cooperation and restraint, communal values tended to outweigh individual freedom.
Leadership was defined less by coercive force than by maintaining balance between human needs and the environment, shaping both daily life and social structure.

sets.name: Unit 03 Reading 2 100세 시대의 비밀을 쥔 유전자
sents: The average global lifespan has doubled in the past century, with people now expected to live over 70 years.
While this is attributed in part to medical advances and better nutrition, experts estimate that genes may determine about half of how long we live.
This has sparked a growing interest in the search for longevity genes, or Methuselah genes, named after the biblical figure who was said to have lived for 969 years.
In 1998, the first longevity gene was identified in fruit flies, with studies showing that flies carrying the gene lived 35 percent longer than those without it.
These flies also exhibited remarkable resilience to environmental stressors, such as extreme heat and food scarcity.
In 2010, German researchers confirmed the existence of a similar longevity gene in humans called FOXO3.
While everyone has this gene, certain variants of it have been found in long-lived individuals worldwide, especially those over 100 years old.
These human gene variants trigger the release of a protein that promotes cell health by eliminating severely damaged cells and repairing less damaged ones, which strengthens the immune system.
Their presence has also been associated with increased resistance to heart disease, stroke, and cancer.
This discovery offers hope for the development of therapies that foster healthy aging and reduce the impact of age-related diseases.

sets.name: Unit 03 Reading 3 파리 올림픽 마스코트의 정체
sents: Since 1968, cities hosting the Olympic Games have introduced mascots to represent them, often choosing animals that symbolize the host city or country in a fun and engaging way.
However, Paris, the host of the 2024 Olympics, selected a hat as the mascot for the Games!
The mascot, Phryge, is a cone-shaped character with lively eyes, a friendly smile, and colorful athletic shoes.
It depicts the iconic Phrygian cap, which is a soft, cone-shaped hat that has been a powerful symbol of freedom in French history since the Revolution.
This red cap was worn by revolutionaries during many critical moments in French history and represents liberty, equality, and fraternity—the core values of the French Republic.
Paris 2024 actually features two Phryges: the Olympic Phryge and the Paralympic Phryge, with the latter wearing a visible prosthetic leg.
This inclusive design choice reflects the Olympic spirit that no one should be excluded based on race, gender, or ability.
The Paralympic Phryge serves as a powerful reminder that the Games celebrate all athletes and promote a world where differences are embraced and valued.
The red cap once worn by revolutionaries in the streets has now taken its place on the Olympic stage before a global audience.
And the ideals of liberty and equality they once fought for became woven into the spirit of the Games, helping define the atmosphere of Paris 2024.

sets.name: Unit 03 Reading 4 Even the Camera Giant Forgot to Run
sents: In Lewis Carroll’s novel Alice Through the Looking-Glass, there is a famous scene involving the Red Queen.
When Alice expresses surprise about remaining in the same spot while running her fastest, the Red Queen tells her that she must run twice as fast to get somewhere else.
This idea, known as the Red Queen effect, applies to the business world.
In the business world, the Red Queen effect is a phenomenon in which companies must constantly improve just to survive, and they must make even greater improvements to achieve further success.
In other words, a company that does not try to adapt to changing market conditions by upgrading its goods and services, regardless of how successful it is, will eventually fail.
This is because there are highly motivated competitors that are constantly improving their products.
A famous example of the Red Queen effect is Kodak, a company that was founded in 1888 and dominated the camera industry as well as the film industry for years.
This brilliant company even went so far as to invent the first digital camera in 1975.
However, Kodak’s executives were concerned that digital cameras might reduce its film sales, so they ultimately decided not to release its invention to the market.
On the other hand, other companies soon developed and released their own digital cameras.
These new products gained tremendous popularity among the public, to such an extent that digital cameras came to dominate the camera market.
As a result, Kodak’s misguided decision led it to declare bankruptcy in 2012.

sets.name: Unit 04 Reading 1 쉿, 근데 다 알잖아~
sents: Employees in an office have gathered for a meeting, but everyone seems distracted and stressed out.
What’s going on?
They must be worried about the elephant in the room.
Of course, it’s not a real elephant.
The expression “elephant in the room” is used to refer to a serious problem that everyone is aware of but no one wants to talk about because it makes them uncomfortable.
In the business world, for example, people may be avoiding mentioning the company’s poor performance or the loss of a major client.
When this happens, some managers choose to take the easy path, that is, ignoring the elephant.
But it often causes adverse consequences, such as leading to low employee morale and a lack of trust in leadership.
Instead, it is best to deal with the elephant as soon as it makes an appearance.
The first step is to acknowledge the issue and raise it with staff members to create an atmosphere in which people feel free to talk openly without fear of criticism.
Next, gather opinions.
Affected individuals need to know that their voices are being heard when it comes to finding a resolution.
Finally, instill confidence by providing a detailed explanation of how the solution will be implemented, making sure to specify the timeline, the intended outcome, and the role of staff members.

sets.name: Unit 04 Reading 2 따로 또 같이, 선집의 매력
sents: Let’s say a group of people decided to produce content exploring the topic of stars.

Each person might take a dramatically different approach depending on their interpretation of the topic, focusing alternately on a girl dreaming of pop stardom, a voyage to a literal star in space, or the discovery of a mysterious star-shaped object.
If the diverse works created by the members of this group were brought together into a collection, it would be called an anthology.
The term comes from the Greek word anthológos, which means “flower-gathering,” a metaphorical reference to the gathering of small poetry verses like flowers in a bouquet.
It was used only in the literary world to describe a group of written works published together in a single volume.
Now, however, it applies to fields such as the visual arts and broadcast media.
In media, one of the most interesting features of an anthology television series is that each episode presents a distinctive story and unique characters that are all connected by a common theme.
In some cases, the episodes might be from different genres—one might be a comedy, the next a thriller, and so on.
With such variety, an anthology series usually attracts a wide audience.
Also, many directors like the creative freedom this type of series provides.
They can take greater risks because they know that viewers who do not care for one episode may come back for another one.
As a result, directors can try out different storytelling and filming techniques in each episode, and they are free to experiment with unusual styles.

sets.name: Unit 04 Reading 3 어둠 속에서도 세상을 꿰뚫어 보는 눈
sents: On a moonless night, a sensor can “see” distinct shapes even without taking a photograph.
It does this by emitting rapid pulses of laser light and timing how long each pulse takes to bounce back.
From these measurements, LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) builds a dense cloud of points that renders detailed 3D images of a place and the objects inside it.
The idea for LiDAR was developed in the United States in the 1960s, soon after lasers were invented.
Its main strength is its reliability across conditions that challenge ordinary cameras.
LiDAR sensors operate as effectively in bright sunlight as in total darkness, and in large, cluttered, or constantly changing environments.
Initially, it was used for tracking targets and studying the atmosphere.
Over time, it became closely tied to earth and environmental sciences because it is ideal for measuring terrain and vegetation.

Airborne LiDAR maps landscapes from above, detecting contours through leaf cover and supporting practical work in forestry, flood-risk modeling, and archaeology, where hidden patterns can appear after the “noise” of plants is digitally removed.
In recent years, LiDAR has also been deployed on autonomous vehicles to scan for objects and estimate distances in real time.
Some smartphones also contain LiDAR sensors that improve camera functions such as focusing or depth effects.
Still, LiDAR is not without drawbacks.
Performance can drop in heavy rain, fog, or snow because the laser pulses can scatter before reaching their target.
LiDAR systems can also be expensive, and their huge data volumes require fast processing.
As LiDAR becomes smaller and cheaper, researchers expect it to enable smarter navigation, precise mapping, and 3D perception.

sets.name: Unit 04 Reading 4 Once Trapped, Now Wrapped
sents: Abandoned fishing equipment—also known as ghost gear—threatens many lives in the ocean.
Over 650,000 marine animals are killed by this form of pollution each year.
Among various types of ghost gear, discarded fishing nets are particularly dangerous.
Any sea creature that becomes caught in a discarded fishing net faces a slow and painful death.
To help address this ecological crisis, a company called Bureo has developed an innovative solution.
Founded by three surfers—Ben Kneppers, David Stover, and Kevin Ahearn—Bureo produces skateboards, sunglasses, and clothing from recycled fishing gear.

The production process goes as follows: initially, the old nets are purchased directly from fishers in countries throughout Central and South America, and local workers are employed to sort and sanitize them.
The processed materials are then transported to a facility in Chile.
There, they are transformed into NetPlus, the 100 percent recycled plastic that is used to make Bureo merchandise.
Thanks to Bureo’s efforts, over 6,000 tonnes of abandoned fishing nets have been transformed into eco-friendly products since 2015.
It goes without saying that many marine animals have been saved from mortal danger!

sets.name: Unit 05 Reading 1 웃는 게 웃는 게 아니야
sents: The saying “Laughter is the best medicine” doesn’t hold true for everyone.
For those with Chronic Laughter Syndrome, laughter can be a source of distress and social difficulty rather than healing.
Chronic Laughter Syndrome, medically referred to as Pseudobulbar Affect (PBA), is a neurological condition characterized by uncontrollable episodes of laughter without appropriate stimuli or context.
These episodes are often exaggerated in intensity and duration, with patients frequently reporting rapid transitions between laughter and crying.
Individuals experiencing the syndrome often face emotional distress and isolation, as they avoid social situations due to their condition.

While the exact cause of PBA is still unknown, experts believe the disorder represents a disruption in emotional regulation that stems from damage to the neural pathways between the cerebral cortex and cerebellum.
The condition is most common in patients who have suffered a stroke or in those experiencing cognitive decline due to dementia.
In the past, treatment options for PBA were highly limited due to its lack of targeted therapies.
However, with the FDA approval of Nuedexta in 2010, clinicians were able to prescribe a medication specifically designed to help manage the condition.
This led to a reported 50 percent reduction in episodes, improving patients’ quality of life and social functioning.

sets.name: Unit 05 Reading 2 피자가 친절하고 사장님이 맛있어요!
sents: Successful conversation is often thought to depend on following certain rules.
Speakers are expected to provide appropriate amounts of information (Quantity), be truthful (Quality), stay relevant (Relation), and communicate clearly (Manner).
Linguist H. P. Grice organized these expectations into four conversational maxims, which describe how cooperative communication works.
It may seem that conversation succeeds only when these maxims are followed, yet in everyday life communication often remains effective even when a maxim is intentionally violated.
Consider a situation in which two adults are discussing dinner while a young child is nearby.
One person asks what to eat, and the other responds by spelling out the name of a fast-food restaurant (for example, “M-C-D-O-N-A-L-D-S”) instead of saying it directly.
The inefficient reply is neither clear nor concise, and it therefore seems to violate a conversational maxim.
Nevertheless, communication does not break down.
Both speakers share the intention of preventing the child from recognizing the word, and the listener infers this intention.
A similar pattern appears when a wife, just waking up, asks, “What time is it?” and her husband replies, “Your alarm hasn’t gone off yet.”
This response does not directly answer the question.
However, the husband is actively signaling that it is still early in the morning.
Even without knowing the exact time, the wife can infer a reasonable estimate based on their shared knowledge of when her alarm usually rings.
In such cases, meaning does not arise from strict obedience to conversational rules.
Instead, communication succeeds when listeners recognize that a rule has been intentionally violated and infer the speaker’s underlying intention.
Conversation, therefore, is not a rigid system that rewards rule-following alone, but a cooperative activity grounded in shared context and interpretation.

sets.name: Unit 05 Reading 3 터치도 하이, 테크도 하이~
sents: Picture this: a classroom filled with active science experiments, students working together in groups on new projects.
Meanwhile, the teacher moves around the classroom, challenging students’ assumptions with thought-provoking questions.
This exemplifies a high-touch learning environment—one that emphasizes personal interaction and emotional engagement between students and teachers.
The concept of high touch is often compared with high-tech education.

While high tech prioritizes efficiency through the use of digital platforms that provide easy and instant access to information, an excessive reliance on devices may result in social isolation and decreased engagement for students.
On the other hand, high-touch classrooms counteract this by immersing students in hands-on activities that promote collaboration and face-to-face communication.
In these classrooms, teachers play a crucial role in fostering interpersonal connections, using real-time interactions to gauge student understanding and adjust their instruction accordingly.
According to experts, the ideal educational approach would be to combine high-touch and high-tech strategies.
This would allow students to learn basic skills through technology, while freeing up teachers to focus on guiding problem-solving activities and leading classroom discussions.

A high-touch, high-tech classroom could also offer a more personalized and comprehensive educational experience, with technology adapting to each student’s progress and teachers responding to emotional needs.

sets.name: Unit 05 Reading 4 From Runway to Ruin
sents: Against the barren landscape of Chile’s Atacama Desert, a fashion show like no other takes place.
Models wearing discarded clothes from Europe, Asia, and North America parade through piles of trash.
The goal of this unusual event is to raise awareness about the ecological issues caused by the massive buildup of textile waste in the region.
The exact amount of clothing dumped in the Atacama Desert remains unknown.
However, estimates suggest that around 39,000 tons are added annually, forming rubbish mounds so massive that they can be seen from space.
Much of the waste is the unsold inventory of major clothing retailers, especially those driving fast-fashion trends.
Out-of-style garments are imported into Chile and then illegally dumped in the desert when they cannot be resold.
The environmental consequences are devastating.
Toxic chemicals from polyester and other synthetic materials seep into the soil and groundwater.
Making matters worse, the discarded clothing sometimes catches fire accidentally or is burned intentionally in an attempt to get rid of it.
In either case, large amounts of pollutants are released into the atmosphere, causing respiratory illnesses and other health problems for area residents.
Although the Chilean government is taking steps to clean up the Atacama Desert, its efforts will have no impact on similar sites sprouting up around the planet.
The only real solution is for consumers to cease consumption of short-lived fashion and pressure the clothing industry into adopting sustainable business practices.

sets.name: Unit 06 Reading 1 멈출 수 없는 춤의 저주
sents: One fairy tale tells the story of a girl who, after putting on red shoes, is forced to dance without stopping.
Surprisingly, there are historical records of nearly identical cases occurring, even affecting whole communities!
In 1518, a woman named Frau Troffea abruptly started dancing in Strasbourg, a city in modern-day France.
She twisted, jumped, and jerked her arms uncontrollably through the streets.

While Troffea’s weird movements in the summer heat terrified many, something peculiar happened: a number of individuals began mirroring her erratic postures, and soon, about 400 men and women were affected by this “dancing plague!”

Local doctors struggled to identify what caused this incomprehensible event, and then finally diagnosed the victims with “hot blood,” a condition they believed resulted from contaminated blood trapped in the body.
To expel the contaminated substance, doctors prescribed a treatment they believed would be effective: more movement.
The city erected stages and hired musicians, and the mania persisted for two months until many collapsed from extreme exhaustion, while some tragically perished from heart attacks or strokes.
This bizarre phenomenon also appeared in other European regions throughout the century.

Today, overwhelming stress is regarded as the most probable cause for the outbreak, as Europeans at the time faced starvation from famine, flooding, multiple contagious diseases, and the constant threat of war.
But lacking definitive evidence, this remains only a theory, leaving the dancing plague an enigma in history.

sets.name: Unit 06 Reading 2 새우도 지구도 포기 못 해
sents: While shrimp is a popular dish around the world, the way it’s traditionally farmed often comes at the expense of nature—destroying coastal ecosystems and polluting nearby waters.
To address these issues, a company called Atarraya has developed an innovative solution—Shrimpbox.
Invented in 2018, the Shrimpbox resembles a shipping container with two large water tanks inside.
Each unit includes fully automated feed dispensers as well as sensors to monitor the temperature, oxygen content, and acidity level of the water.
These complex systems are controlled by artificial intelligence (AI), with the aim of optimizing conditions for shrimp production.
The technology has proven highly effective, with a single Shrimpbox capable of producing up to 1,500 kilograms of shrimp annually with little human involvement.
Perhaps the most significant advantage of Shrimpbox is that it minimizes the environmental impact of shrimp farming.
This is primarily achieved by employing a recirculating aquaculture system (RAS), which recycles over 95 percent of the water.
Furthermore, harmful chemicals do not need to be added to keep the water clean because the tanks used in the system include special algae that consume the waste produced by the shrimp.
The end result is that the Shrimpbox uses a smaller amount of natural resources and produces fewer ecologically harmful byproducts than a conventional shrimp farm.

sets.name: Unit 06 Reading 3 생일보다 더 중요한 날이 있다?!
sents: A Greek girl named Sofia is surrounded by loved ones wishing her well and offering her delicious foods, even though it’s not her birthday.
What’s the occasion?
It’s her name day!
A name day is the celebration of a saint someone is named after.
The Greek Orthodox Church follows a calendar dedicated to saints, with almost every day honoring at least one of them.
Since Greece is a deeply Christian country, with approximately 90 percent of the population adhering to Christianity, the majority of Greeks are named after saints.
Traditionally, you host an “open home,” letting friends and family visit.
Guests bring food and drinks and give you gifts such as flowers symbolizing your name or birth season, or a small icon featuring the saint you were named after.
For Greek Orthodox Christians, their name day is more significant than their birthday.
It’s a way to strengthen their relationship with God and honor the saint after whom they are named.
Interestingly, many Greek elderly don’t even know their exact birthdate, but only their name day.
While forgetting an individual’s birthday is generally deemed permissible in Greece, committing a similar oversight on their name day is considered highly discourteous.
To properly acknowledge this vital occasion, it’s customary to wish them a Chronia Polla, an expression of goodwill and health.

sets.name: Unit 06 Reading 4 Built for the Hunt, Broken by the Desk
sents: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is characterized by impulsivity, hyperactivity, and inattention.
While often seen as negative today, ADHD-related traits may have offered evolutionary advantages in past environments.

According to the “hunter versus farmer” hypothesis in evolutionary psychiatry, individuals with ADHD traits may have been better suited to nomadic hunter-gatherer societies, where the ability to quickly adapt and respond to environmental stimuli was essential.
A study published in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B investigated this idea by having participants play an online berry-picking game.
The test results indicated that participants who self-reported ADHD behaviors demonstrated greater efficiency in foraging scenarios requiring constant movement and swift decision-making.
In situations designed to mimic the conditions faced by ancient gatherers, they were quicker to abandon depleted berry patches and gathered more berries overall compared to those without such traits.

These evolutionary insights imply that the prevalence of ADHD traits in modern populations—found in 11 percent of children and 4 percent of adults—could be remnants of adaptive behaviors from our nomadic lifestyles in ancient hunter-gatherer societies.
With the advent of sedentary agricultural societies, the same traits may have become less compatible with structured, repetitive tasks.
Understanding this evolutionary context can provide a more nuanced view of ADHD, recognizing that behaviors deemed problematic today may have once played a crucial role in human survival.

sets.name: Unit 07 Reading 1 옷장은 가볍게, 스타일은 완벽하게
sents: Do you have lots of clothes but still feel like you have nothing to wear?
A capsule wardrobe would be the best solution for you; it is a curated collection of just 10 to 20 interchangeable clothing items designed to maximize outfit options while minimizing clutter.

This minimalist fashion approach originated in the 1970s when Susie Faux introduced the concept at her London boutique, Wardrobe, after noticing that customers were spending money on low-quality, trendy pieces that quickly went out of style.
The idea gained mainstream popularity in 1985 when designer Donna Karan released her “Seven Easy Pieces” collection, featuring versatile items for working women to wear for any occasion.
Building your own capsule wardrobe is straightforward.
Begin by auditing your closet—identify the pieces you love and wear regularly, and resolutely get rid of the rest.
If you need to add items, invest in high-quality pieces with timeless designs in neutral colors that mix and match easily and can be dressed up or down.
The benefits extend beyond a tidy closet.
A capsule wardrobe saves time by eliminating decision fatigue, minimizes expenses by reducing impulse purchases, and helps the environment by encouraging sustainable consumption.

sets.name: Unit 07 Reading 2 경계가 사라진 세상
sents: Netflix is entering the game industry, Tesla sells insurance products, and Sony makes cars.
These all exemplify the “Big Blur” phenomenon.
First introduced by Stan Davis and Christopher Meyer in 1999, the term refers to the blurring of industry boundaries, where once-distinct sectors now overlap.
In the past, companies specialized in narrowly defined fields: banks handled money, media agencies produced entertainment.
But with the emergence of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, a new era of living and working driven by artificial intelligence and cloud computing, those boundaries started to fade.
Hospitals utilize AI algorithms to detect potential health complications, while tech firms like Google provide health-tracking services once exclusive to medical institutions.

While the Big Blur offers new opportunities for innovation and job creation, organizations face competition not only from traditional rivals but also from new entrants originating from different industries.
It is thus important for businesses to remain adaptable and open to integration.
In a Big Blur society, the ability to think across disciplines is just as valuable as deep expertise.
The Big Blur may be influencing not only industries, but also the kinds of skills and ways of thinking people value.
As boundaries continue to fade, the ability to adapt and connect ideas across different fields may gradually become more valuable as well.

sets.name: Unit 07 Reading 3 아무리 그래도 챙길 건 챙겨야지!
sents: For several hundred years, the pharaohs, the kings of ancient Egypt, were buried in elaborate and ornate tombs located in an area that has come to be known as the Valley of the Kings.
In 1170 BC, the artisans who were tasked with building and decorating these burial sites chose a course of action that would have been unthinkable at the time.
Having waited 18 days to receive their regular payment of grain, which the workers typically used to make bread as their main food source, they laid down their tools and refused to work.
Instead of performing their assigned tasks, they marched to the local officials and proclaimed, “We are hungry!”
The workers’ demands were simple: they would only resume their duties when they received payment for the work they had already completed.
Wanting progress on the tombs to continue, the officials mandated that bread be delivered to the men.
Because the workers considered their offer to be acceptable, they returned to their work the next day.
After that incident, the workers continued to strike whenever they felt they were being exploited, which put pressure on the officials to give them full rations and fair treatment.
Eventually, they had to yield to the workers’ demands.
For the first time in history, workers proved what could be accomplished when they stood up for themselves, establishing a precedent for others to follow.

sets.name: Unit 07 Reading 4 Counting Without Counting
sents: In popular music, as well as in classical and jazz, melodies often unfold in units of four beats.
A musical phrase is commonly built from four measures, which may then expand into eight.
Listeners do not consciously count these numbers, but they still have a natural sense of what comes next.
Performers experience this feeling as well, relying more on intuition than calculation to know when to begin and when to conclude.
This profound stability originates not intrinsically from music itself, but from the fundamental mechanisms governing human locomotion and cognition.
Human movement follows paired rhythms, such as walking and breathing, which naturally group in twos.
As these patterns expand, four and eight become the most comfortable units for the body to follow.
The brain seems to favor this structure too, as four beats are long enough to register as a pattern yet short enough to maintain tension, while eight beats provide a sense of completion.
By contrast, odd-numbered rhythms often feel unstable and demand greater attention from the listener.
For this reason, not all music aims for stability alone.
Jazz and experimental music frequently use irregular rhythms to introduce tension and movement.
These effects stand out, however, precisely because a familiar four-beat structure already exists as a reference.
In the end, music feels stable in fours and eights not because the numbers themselves are special, but because human bodies and brains already move and think in such rhythms.
Music does not simply follow numbers; rather, it reflects human perception.

sets.name: Unit 08 Reading 1 말 한마디에 AI가 달라져!
sents: Artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally reshaping the job market, with routine tasks increasingly being automated.
Simultaneously, new careers in the AI industry are emerging, such as prompt engineering.
Prompt engineering is the practice of designing and refining specific instructions—called “prompts”—for AI programs in order to generate appropriate outputs.
Skillfully crafted prompts enhance the performance of AI, greatly increasing its utility for a wide variety of applications, including content creation, data analysis, and problem-solving.
Effective prompt engineering involves several key elements.
Most importantly, the task must be accurately explained with precise language that avoids any ambiguous phrasing.
The prompt should also contain the context necessary for the AI program to comprehend the anticipated outcome.
This might take the form of relevant background information, concrete examples, or a comprehensive set of parameters.
Finally, the prompt should identify the desired format and tone of the response to make certain that it corresponds to the user’s expectations.
AI is a powerful tool capable of generating a vast amount of data at a remarkable speed.
However, the quality of its output is dependent on the input it receives from the user.
The more sophisticated the input is, the more effective the AI becomes.

sets.name: Unit 08 Reading 2 공식 스폰서인 척 숟가락 얹기!
sents: Coca-Cola was the official sponsor of the 2014 soccer World Cup, the biggest sporting event on the planet.
In response, Pepsi launched a campaign featuring popular soccer players whose faces appeared on special edition Pepsi cans.
Through this smart strategy, it managed to reap substantial benefits from the World Cup fever, despite having no legitimate connection to the event.
This is called ambush marketing, where a brand uses creative campaigns to associate itself with a major event and thus gain attention without actually paying for sponsorships.
This technique has two approaches—direct and indirect.
A direct ambush makes explicit references to an event or competitor.
For instance, Visa paid $40 million to be the official credit card of the 1994 Winter Olympics in Norway.
However, its rival American Express ran an ambush campaign with the tagline, “If you’re traveling to Norway, you’ll need a passport, but you don’t need a visa.”
This clever play on words undermined Visa’s reputation on the global stage while drawing attention to American Express.
Indirect ambush marketing, on the other hand, is much more subtle.
Before the 2012 London Olympics, Beats by Dre, a well-known audio equipment company, strategically distributed custom headphones featuring the flags of various countries to athletes.
Many participants wore them during the TV broadcast, and this widespread exposure contributed significantly to a 42 percent increase in sales that year.
However, ambush marketing should be employed with extreme caution, as it can lead to severe risks.
Illegally using an event’s intellectual property, such as logos or related slogans, could result in heavy fines and could also damage the company’s reputation.

sets.name: Unit 08 Reading 3 환경을 위해 태어난 거였어?
sents: Because single-use plastic bags are known to cause irreparable environmental damage, using reusable bags to carry groceries home from the supermarket has become the norm.
However, you may be surprised to learn that plastic bags were first developed as a green alternative.
In 1965, the Swedish engineer Sten Thulin invented plastic bags to reduce people’s reliance on paper bags.
At the time, most stores provided customers with paper bags, and many trees were cut down annually to produce them.
By switching to plastic, Thulin hoped his invention would slow the process of deforestation and provide a reusable alternative for carrying goods.
While plastic bags proved popular, making up 80 percent of Europe’s shopping bag market by 1979, people did not follow Thulin’s intention.
They discarded the bags after a single use, resulting in millions of plastic bags being added to landfills each year.
This accumulation of waste sparked the eventual shift to reusable bags made from sturdier synthetic materials or natural fibers like cotton or hemp.
The widespread adoption and eventual rejection of plastic bags illustrates an underlying truth about scientific progress—inventions meant to benefit humanity often have unintended negative effects.
It is thus imperative for the scientific community to fully understand the potential impact of new technologies before they are made available to the public.

sets.name: Unit 08 Reading 4 The Illusion of the Better Deal
sents: Imagine being offered two choices: receive $10 now or $100 after a year.
While the second option is more rational, many people would choose the immediate reward due to a cognitive bias called hyperbolic discounting.
This flawed decision-making process is characterized by a preference for instant gratification, even when waiting would lead to a better outcome.

Psychologists have identified two causes of this behavior, with the first being that people are naturally risk-averse; concern about the future availability of the greater reward makes them more inclined to accept the smaller one.
Another factor is that waiting triggers feelings of anxiety and frustration.
Unless a person has a high level of self-discipline, the option that does not require patience will almost always be selected.
Hyperbolic discounting has roots that trace back to early humans, with some scientists arguing it was an evolutionary advantage.
They lived in a world where access to vital resources such as food and clean water was highly unpredictable.
Immediate consumption ensured survival, while delay resulted in a missed opportunity to secure what was needed.
Over time, this preference for short-term rewards became ingrained in human cognition, persisting even in modern societies where long-term planning is often the key to success.

sets.name: Unit 09 Reading 1 화가 나면 왜 말이 꼬일까?
sents: Our desire to logically explain our feelings intensifies when we’re angry.
However, finding the right words to communicate effectively in these moments frequently proves challenging.
When we experience anger, the amygdala, the brain region that processes emotions, quickly triggers an automatic stress response in our bodies.

During this process, stress hormones like adrenaline and cortisol flood the body to increase heart rate, blood pressure, and muscle tension, giving us extra energy to either face or flee the source of our anger.
With so much energy directed to the body, the prefrontal cortex, which is responsible for reasoning and decision-making, becomes temporarily impaired.
As a result, when angry, this part of the brain is “turned off,” making it hard to communicate in a rational way.
This is why psychologists recommend stepping away from a situation as soon as you start feeling angry.
Giving yourself time to calm down and exit the fight-or-flight mode allows the prefrontal cortex to “turn back on,” so you can express yourself clearly.
In short, taking a step back is not about dismissing your anger, but about controlling it to formulate the most brilliant and logical argument possible.

sets.name: Unit 09 Reading 2 세상에 단 하나! 근데 가치는 보장 못 함?
sents: In 2021, an artwork titled Everydays: The First 5000 Days was sold for approximately $69 million.
Given the high cost, you might be surprised to learn it is not a painting by a famous artist, but rather a digital image.
This work of art utilizes a revolutionary technology called a non-fungible token (NFT) to guarantee its uniqueness.

An NFT is a digital identifier that is recorded on a blockchain to ensure it cannot be duplicated and then associated with a single digital asset to certify its authenticity—a process known as tokenization.

From images to video clips to audio recordings, it is possible to tokenize almost any type of digital file to create a one-of-a-kind item that can be transferred from seller to buyer securely and conveniently.

While the development of NFT technology has been hyped as an exciting new method for digital creators to monetize their work, many experts have taken a more skeptical view, arguing that it has resulted in risky speculation.
Investors have shown themselves willing to pay excessively high prices for NFT art in the hope of significant profits down the road, only to suffer severe financial losses.
For example, Bored Ape #8817—an NFT image of a golden-furred ape wearing a funny hat—sold for a whopping $3.4 million in 2021.
However, the prices of other NFTs in the Bored Ape series have plummeted, and Bored Ape #8817 is now valued at only around $600,000.

sets.name: Unit 09 Reading 3 지금 이 감각이 진짜일까?
sents: Can we truly trust what we see, hear, or feel?
Do our senses provide an answer to how we comprehend the world?
The French philosopher René Descartes explored this very idea through his famous wax argument.
This 17th-century thinker, considered the father of modern Western philosophy, was highly doubtful of knowledge gained by any means other than reason.
He even went so far as to claim that we cannot trust the information gathered by our senses.
To illustrate the unreliability of the senses, Descartes developed the wax argument in his Meditations on First Philosophy.
In this work, Descartes describes in great detail the physical characteristics of a piece of wax—its texture, color, shape, and smell.
He then points out that when the wax is heated to the melting point, all of these qualities are fundamentally altered.
And yet he is still able to identify it as wax.
Descartes concludes that true understanding is rooted in the mind, not in sensory experience, reinforcing his famous claim: Cogito, ergo sum—“I think, therefore I am.”
By emphasizing reason as the basis of knowledge, he challenges the idea that perception alone can lead to certainty.
His insights laid the groundwork for modern rationalism, shaping debates on the nature of knowledge and the reliability of human perception for centuries to come.

sets.name: Unit 09 Reading 4 Loading... Answer Not Found
sents: You may know that feeling when a word is on the tip of your tongue; you definitely know it, but you just can’t say it.
This frustrating situation is an example of the Feeling of Knowing.
The Feeling of Knowing refers to being unable to retrieve information from memory, even though you believe you can.
While experiencing it, you intuitively sense that with just a little more time or different circumstances, the information will surely come to you.
Where does the Feeling of Knowing come from?
According to several scientific studies, it’s related to having partial information about the given question.
In short, the more partial information you have, the stronger your Feeling of Knowing will be.
For example, you are shown the face of a celebrity and asked to give their name.
You recognize the face, but the name doesn’t come to you.
Brain scans taken during such moments have shown that the medial prefrontal cortex, a region of the brain critically involved in long-term memory retrieval, activates.
This area has two key functions: First, it cycles through the partial information you do remember about the subject (in this case, the celebrity).
Second, it evaluates whether the information you are retrieving is relevant to the question.
If no correct answer emerges from this largely unconscious process, you’re left with nothing but the Feeling of Knowing.

sets.name: Unit 10 Reading 1 내 심장 소리가 들려
sents: The Guinness World Record for the quietest place on Earth is held by a special room called an anechoic chamber, where it is so silent that you can hear your heart beating, your blood flowing, and your bones grinding.
The experience is very disorienting, and no one has ever been able to stay inside an anechoic chamber for much longer than an hour.
External noises cannot penetrate the chamber because it is constructed of steel and concrete layers and is supported by springs that prevent vibrations.
Heavy doors sealed with rubber gaskets keep outside air to a minimum.
Even the external passageway will be attached only to the room’s outer shell to stop vibrations from people’s steps from causing interference.
But the most impressive feature is the design of the interior, which guarantees that any sound in the room is stifled.
This effect is achieved through the use of wedges made of sound-absorbent material.
These stick out from all parts of the internal walls, floor, and ceiling, so sound waves generated inside the chamber almost immediately strike one.
When this occurs, most of the sound waves are absorbed, and the angle of the wedge ensures that any reflected waves end up hitting an adjacent wedge.
The process repeats itself until the sound waves are eliminated, resulting in total silence for anyone standing at the chamber’s center.
This is where the chamber’s name comes from—anechoic means “no echo.”

sets.name: Unit 10 Reading 2 유리 빌딩 보면서 불안했던 사람 손
sents: The sight of sunlight glinting off the glass surfaces of skyscrapers is prevalent in urban areas.
But how can these massive structures have walls made of such a fragile material?
It is because the exterior glass is not actually a structural component of the building—it is a thin covering known as a curtain wall.
This architectural element takes its name from the fact that it is attached to the outer part of a building, hanging almost like a curtain.
In contrast to a conventional wall, it does not bear any weight.
Typically made of aluminum frames with glass panels, curtain walls form a lightweight skin designed to be visually pleasing.
Of course, their purpose extends beyond appearance.
They offer protection against harsh weather by shielding the structure from rain, snow, and wind.
Another key function is improving energy efficiency—the glass is typically coated with substances that enhance insulation and regulate incoming sunlight.
This makes it easier to maintain interior temperatures, which reduces heating and cooling costs.
A striking example of this technology is the Burj Khalifa in Dubai.
Rising to a height of 828 meters, this iconic tower features a curtain wall composed of approximately 28,000 glass panels.

These are treated with a reflective coating that permits only 20 percent of the intense desert sunlight to enter, protecting occupants from the heat and glare while creating an aesthetically pleasing façade.

sets.name: Unit 10 Reading 3 위궤양의 범인은 대체 누구야?
sents: Imagine risking your own health to make a medical breakthrough.
That’s precisely what Australian doctor Barry Marshall did.
In 1981, Marshall and his colleague, Robin Warren, conducted research on stomach ulcers, a condition that affected 10 percent of the world’s population at that time.
They discovered high concentrations of a bacterium called H. pylori near ulcer sites, leading Marshall to hypothesize that these bacteria caused ulcers.
However, he had to disprove a long-held assumption about ulcers; namely, that this condition was the result of excess stomach acid caused by stress, spicy food, or smoking.
To prove his theory, Marshall attempted to infect animals with H. pylori, but the bacteria could not survive in most animal stomachs.
Although he was frustrated by this failure, he was still confident in his hypothesis and decided to test it on himself.
He drank a broth containing H. pylori and, within days, developed the symptoms of gastritis, a precursor to ulcers.
His condition soon progressed to a full-blown stomach ulcer, which he successfully cured with antibiotics.
Being able to treat ulcers with medication was groundbreaking at the time, as severe cases sometimes required surgery to remove parts of the stomach.
For his contribution to science, Marshall won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

sets.name: Unit 10 Reading 4 Disappearing to Start Over
sents: Have you ever considered disappearing from society entirely, leaving everything behind to start fresh?
In Japan, this idea is a reality for many who choose to undergo Jouhatsu, or human evaporation.
This phenomenon allows individuals to escape the pressures of modern society, often driven by overwhelming shame or societal expectations, and essentially reset their lives.
Jouhatsu originated in the 1960s, as a way for people to leave unhappy marriages without having to deal with the social stigma often tied to divorce at the time.
During Japan’s severe economic downturn in the 1990s, this practice became more prevalent as people chose to evaporate to avoid financial ruin.
Today, about 100,000 people in Japan evaporate annually; the most common reasons include financial difficulties, job loss, and relationship issues.
Many pay companies that offer night moving services to help them disappear, with costs varying depending on the number of people involved, how many possessions they have, and how far they wish to go.
The vanished people are moved to a new area with a new name to begin their new life.
As this process exists in a legal gray area, authorities have no grounds for investigating cases of Jouhatsu.
Despite the seemingly complete erasure of their past lives, Jouhatsu does not always lead to a fresh start.
Some individuals find themselves trapped in a cycle of instability, struggling to move forward under the weight of their unresolved pasts.
The families left behind also suffer the emotional toll of these decisions, unable to find closure or understand why their loved ones vanished.
